title: Health Checks and Service Recovery
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of health checks and service recovery.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to health checks and service recovery.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Health Checks and Service Recovery. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Docker Compose describes a multi-service application declaratively. It can define images/builds, networks, volumes, environment, health checks, and dependencies; startup order alone does not guarantee that a dependency is ready to accept requests. Learning health checks and service recovery helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Health-check design
items.text: Operational signals should help answer what failed, when it failed, and what changed. Establish a baseline and record the checks used to decide that the service recovered.

items.title: Startup failure handling
items.text: For startup failure handling, name the relevant Docker object, setting, or operational step; predict its effect; and capture evidence from a controlled test or inspection command. Relate the result back to health checks and service recovery rather than assuming that a successful command proves the wider system is correct.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for health checks and service recovery. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Health Checks and Service Recovery
content_blocks.code:
docker ps -a
docker logs --tail 50 CONTAINER_NAME
docker inspect CONTAINER_NAME
content_blocks.expected_output: The commands show container state, recent application output, and the inspectable runtime configuration for a chosen container.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Replace CONTAINER_NAME with a container from your disposable lab. Preserve the exact error text before changing settings.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Read-only diagnostics; no reset is required.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
